[RCLI.3.1] **Four exit codes, and they are a contract.**

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | success |
| `1` | compile error — the program was refused, and one or more diagnostics rendered to stderr |
| `2` | usage error — the invocation did not parse against `compiler/dsc_cli.ebnf` and used none of this compiler's own options or subcommands ([RCLI.1.3]), named an option this edition does not admit ([RCLI.2.1]) or this compiler does not implement, named a path that could not be read or written, or found no bundled library ([RCLI.1.11]) |
| `3` | internal compiler error — the compiler failed while carrying out an invocation it had accepted: a fault in the compiler, or its memory exhausted |

The distinction between `1` and `2` is what a build script branches on: a
compile error means the program is wrong, a usage error means the command was.
Collapsing them would make a mistyped flag indistinguishable from a rejected
program.

A `3` is the compiler's fault, never the program's or the command's. A compiler that finds it cannot finish what an invocation
asks **must** exit `3`, write the reason to stderr, and write none of the
artefact it could not finish: no byte of it to standard output, and no file at
the path `-o` names. [RCLI.1.4] states which artefacts `compile-project` keeps
when it stops. It renders no diagnostic, since it reaches no verdict on the
program.

A compiler must refuse an option it does not implement, with `2`, rather than
accept and ignore it: an ignored option hands back an artefact the author
believes carries something it does not.
